title: 10.6 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can look back at my answers from Lesson 1-1, describe how my math biography has changed this year, and recognize ways we are all doers of math, explain how I can tell, and judge a case I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

turnAndTalk.kernel: 80 riders per turn × 6 turns an hour = 480 riders an hour, using a rate — a tool this year's math added.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 10.6. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Your math story, one year later
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: We are all doers of math and use math in our daily lives. Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me reread my September work
lines: In September I estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4 = 80 riders — 'about 80.'
Now I can go further with this year's math: at 6 turns an hour, that wheel moves about 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour.
Same wheel, same me — but my toolbox grew. That difference IS my math story.
linesEs: En septiembre estimé la rueda de la fortuna: 20 cabinas con unas 4 personas cada una son 20 × 4 = 80 personas — «unas 80».
Ahora puedo ir más lejos con las matemáticas de este año: a 6 vueltas por hora, esa rueda mueve unas 80 × 6 = 480 personas por hora.
La misma rueda, el mismo yo — pero mi caja de herramientas creció. Esa diferencia es mi historia matemática.
iDo.titleEs: Mírame releer mi trabajo de septiembre

weDo.title: Try it together — then prove it
lines: In September we decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5 and 80 − 1.5.
This year we learned new ways to say the same number: 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2.
Find one more way to write 78.5 using something you learned this year.
Now prove it: say why that move had to work at all — not just that it did.
Sentence frame — convince a skeptic: "My method works because ___ . It would stop working if ___ ."
linesEs: Este año aprendimos maneras nuevas de decir el mismo número: 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2.
Halla una manera más de escribir 78.5 usando algo que hayas aprendido este año.
Ahora demuéstralo: di por qué ese paso tenía que funcionar — no solo que funcionó.
Marco de oración — convence a alguien que duda: «Mi método funciona porque ___ . Dejaría de funcionar si ___ .»

youDo.title: Now you try — and defend it
lines: Try the problems below on your own. Getting the answer is half the work — be ready to say why your method works, and where it would stop working.
Then pick one problem and show it a second way. If two different methods agree, that agreement is your proof.
linesEs: Intenta los problemas de abajo por tu cuenta. Obtener la respuesta es la mitad del trabajo — prepárate para decir por qué funciona tu método y dónde dejaría de funcionar.
Luego elige un problema y muéstralo de una segunda manera. Si dos métodos distintos coinciden, esa coincidencia es tu prueba.

interactiveVisual.label: Write the same number a different way, then check it.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Ve más allá — Tu historia matemática, un año después
conceptIntro.introEs: Esto ya lo sabes hacer. Así que subimos de nivel, no de número: halla lo que siempre es cierto, muéstralo de una segunda manera y prepárate para defenderlo con una razón en lugar de una respuesta.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Todos hacemos matemáticas y las usamos en la vida diaria. Nuestras historias matemáticas siguen creciendo y cambiando conforme crecemos y avanzamos — y puedes decir por qué es cierto y dónde dejaría de serlo.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: The September cards come straight from Lesson 1-1 — you were already a doer of math before this year started. The Grade 6 cards are what this year added. After sorting, tell a partner which new skill you have actually used outside of class. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

connect.scenario: You and your classmates each wrote about your math stories at the beginning of the school year. Everyone has their own math story, and as you encounter new challenges and experiences, your story might change.
connect.promptQuestion: How does your classmate's end-of-school-year math story compare to your story?
connect.prompt: Describe how your math story has ___ this year, ask a ___ about their story, and then ___ the two to see how they are alike and different.

check.stem: In September you estimated the Ferris wheel as 20 cars × 4 riders = about 80. Which of these uses a tool you did NOT have in September to extend that same estimate?
choices: Multiplying the 80 riders per turn by 6 turns per hour to find a rate of 480 riders per hour
Adding the 20 cars and 4 riders together to get 24
Guessing a completely different, unrelated number
Deciding not to estimate the Ferris wheel at all
check.explanation: 80 × 6 = 480 uses a rate, a tool this year's math added — the September estimate of 20 × 4 could not do this. Adding 20 + 4 or guessing does not use any new math tool at all.

check.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a real comparison of math stories with a classmate from just repeating what you already believe?
choices: Naming something the classmate actually said, plus one genuine similarity AND one genuine difference between the two stories
Writing 'we both got better at math' and stopping there
Copying your own September answer word for word
Skipping the classmate entirely and writing only about yourself
check.explanation: The check asks for something the classmate actually said. It also asks you to name a genuine similarity. And a genuine difference. “We both got better” shows none of that, so it does not prove a real conversation happened.

check.stem: A student writes, 'My classmate's story changed the same way mine did — we both feel more confident now.' What is missing from this comparison?
choices: A genuine DIFFERENCE between the two stories, not just a shared similarity
The classmate's full name and grade
The exact date Lesson 1-1 was taught
A drawing of the Ferris wheel
check.explanation: A complete comparison names two things. It names a similarity. It also names a difference. This answer gives only a similarity, so it does not meet the lesson's check.

connect.modelAnswer: My classmate said that in September he only felt safe in math when he could copy an example, and now he tries problems first and checks the example after. We both got more comfortable being wrong on a first try. But our stories differ: his confidence grew most in equations, while mine grew most in ratios, because I started using unit rates when I shop with my mom.

onLevel.stem: Now stretch the September estimate with this year's math: about 80 riders per turn, 6 turns each hour. About how many riders per hour?
choices: About 480
About 86
About 13
About 800
onLevel.explanation: 80 riders on each of 6 turns is 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour — a rate, one of this year's tools.
choiceFeedback: That divides 80 by 6 instead of multiplying.
hints: Each turn carries a full load of about 80.
There are 6 turns in an hour.
onLevel.stemEs: Ahora amplía la estimación de septiembre con las matemáticas de este año: unos 80 pasajeros por vuelta, 6 vueltas por hora. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros por hora?
onLevel.explanationEs: 80 pasajeros en cada una de 6 vueltas es 80 × 6 = 480 pasajeros por hora — una tasa, una de las herramientas de este año.
hintsEs: Cada vuelta lleva una carga completa de unos 80.
Hay 6 vueltas en una hora.

onLevel.stem: Percents were new this year. What is 50% of 157?
onLevel.explanation: 50% means half, and 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — the very number you decomposed back in Lesson 1-1.
choiceFeedback: 107 subtracts 50 from 157 instead of taking 50 percent.
hints: 50% of a number is half of it.
Half of 157 means 157 ÷ 2.
Check your answer by doubling it — you should land back on 157.
onLevel.stemEs: Los porcentajes fueron nuevos este año. ¿Cuánto es el 50% de 157?
onLevel.explanationEs: 50% significa la mitad, y 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — el mismo número que descompusiste en la Lección 1-1.
hintsEs: El 50% de un número es su mitad.
La mitad de 157 significa 157 ÷ 2.
Revisa tu respuesta duplicándola — debes volver a 157.

onLevel.stem: What challenges did you face in math this year, and how did you respond to these challenges?
onLevel.modelAnswer: Dividing fractions was my biggest challenge — my first quiz did not go well. I responded by drawing models before using the rule, and by asking my partner to explain her way. By the next unit I could explain WHY dividing by one-half doubles a number.
sentenceStems: My biggest challenge this year was ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Qué retos enfrentaste en matemáticas este año, y cómo respondiste a esos retos?
sentenceStemsEs: Mi mayor desafío este año fue ___ .

onLevel.stem: Which of these is the strongest evidence that YOUR math reasoning grew this year?
choices: You can explain why a method works, not just follow its steps
You finish worksheets faster than in September
You memorized more answers than before
You stopped making any mistakes
onLevel.explanation: Constructing and explaining reasoning is the growth this lesson asks you to look for — it is what makes the math yours.
choiceFeedback: Speed can grow without understanding growing — it is not evidence of reasoning.
Memorized answers work only on problems you have already seen; reasoning works on new ones.
Nobody stopped making mistakes — growth shows in how you respond to them.
hints: Think about reasoning, not speed or memory.
Which option is about understanding WHY?
Explaining why a method works shows the math is yours.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es la evidencia más fuerte de que TU razonamiento matemático creció este año?
onLevel.explanationEs: Construir y explicar tu razonamiento es el crecimiento que esta lección te pide buscar — es lo que hace que las matemáticas sean tuyas.
hintsEs: Piensa en el razonamiento, no en la rapidez ni en la memoria.
¿Cuál opción se trata de entender POR QUÉ?
Explicar por qué funciona un método muestra que las matemáticas son tuyas.
choicesEs: Puedes explicar por qué funciona un método, no solo seguir sus pasos
Terminas las hojas de trabajo más rápido que en septiembre

extending.label: Answer each quick problem with this year's skills — the same numbers you met in Lesson 1-1.
extending.labelEs: Responde cada problema rápido con las destrezas de este año: los mismos números que viste en la Lección 1-1.

rows.problem: Riders per hour: 80 per turn × 6 turns

hints: 50% is a half; 10% moves the decimal one place left.
The Ferris wheel numbers are from your September estimate — solve them with June skills.
hintsEs: 50% es la mitad; 10% mueve el decimal un lugar a la izquierda.
Los números de la rueda de la fortuna son de tu estimación de septiembre: resuélvelos con destrezas de junio.
extending.explanation: Half of 157 is 78.5 — the very number Lesson 1-1 asked you to decompose in September. 10% of 480 moves the decimal to 48, and the Ferris wheel still carries 80 × 6 = 480 riders an hour. Same numbers, new power: that difference is the portfolio's evidence of growth.
extending.explanationEs: La mitad de 157 es 78.5, el mismísimo número que la Lección 1-1 te pidió descomponer en septiembre. El 10% de 480 mueve el decimal a 48, y la rueda de la fortuna sigue llevando 80 × 6 = 480 pasajeros por hora. Los mismos números con un poder nuevo: esa diferencia es la evidencia de crecimiento del portafolio.

extending.label: Match each September estimate to the refined result your math produces now.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada estimación de septiembre con el resultado refinado que tus matemáticas producen ahora.
hints: Each left card is a September question; each right card is where this year's skills take it.
Chain the estimates: riders per turn → riders per hour → riders per evening.
hintsEs: Cada tarjeta izquierda es una pregunta de septiembre; cada derecha es adonde la llevan las destrezas de este año.
Encadena las estimaciones: pasajeros por vuelta → por hora → por noche.
extending.explanation: The chain runs from first estimate to full answer: 20 × 4 gives about 80 riders per turn, 80 × 6 gives 480 an hour, and 3 hours carries 1,440 riders — while the place-value decomposition of 78.5 shows the precision you now attach to a number you once only estimated. The September questions did not change; the mathematician did.
extending.explanationEs: La cadena va de la primera estimación a la respuesta completa: 20 × 4 da unos 80 pasajeros por vuelta, 80 × 6 da 480 por hora y 3 horas llevan a 1,440 pasajeros, mientras que la descomposición por valor posicional de 78.5 muestra la precisión que ahora le pones a un número que antes solo estimabas. Las preguntas de septiembre no cambiaron; quien cambió fue el matemático.

extending.stem: Ask a classmate about their math story. How has your classmate's math story changed since the beginning of the year?
extending.modelAnswer: My classmate told me she used to erase everything the moment it looked wrong. Now she keeps her first attempt and writes the fix next to it, because seeing the mistake helped her on the ratio unit. Her story changed from hiding mistakes to using them.

extending.modelAnswer: I am most confident with ratios and unit rates now — I can set up a table and trust it. My strengths are estimating before I solve, which I already had in September, and explaining my steps out loud, which grew this year.

extending.stem: Which set shows THREE correct ways to write 78.5 using skills from this year?
extending.explanation: All three rebuild 78.5 exactly: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, 50% of 157 = 78.5, and 78½ = 78.5.
choiceFeedback: 78¼ = 78.25, so that set contains an error.
156 ÷ 2 = 78, so that set contains an error.
25% of 157 = 39.25, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set against 78.5.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all three land exactly on 78.5.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál conjunto muestra TRES maneras correctas de escribir 78.5 usando destrezas de este año?
extending.explanationEs: Las tres reconstruyen 78.5 exactamente: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, 50% de 157 = 78.5, y 78½ = 78.5.
hintsEs: Revisa cada miembro de cada conjunto contra 78.5.
Un solo miembro incorrecto arruina todo el conjunto.
Halla el conjunto donde las tres caen exactamente en 78.5.

extending.stem: How have your math thinking HABITS changed from the beginning of the year to now? (Not what you know — how you think.)
extending.modelAnswer: In September my habit was to answer fast and move on. Now my habits are to estimate first so I can judge my answer, to try a second strategy when the first stalls, and to ask 'does this make sense?' before calling anything done. The facts I learned may fade, but I think these habits will stay.

extending.stem: Write a short letter to your September self. Tell them one thing about their math story that will change, and one piece of advice for the year ahead.
extending.modelAnswer: Dear September me: right now you think 'about 80 riders' is the best you can do with that Ferris wheel — by June you will turn it into 480 riders per hour without blinking. My advice: when the fraction unit gets hard in the winter, do not erase your wrong answers. You are going to learn more from them than from the right ones.

extending.stem: We are always growing and changing. Think about who you were five years ago and who you are now. In what ways have you changed? In what ways have you grown?
extending.modelAnswer: Five years ago I was learning to multiply and I needed someone to tell me if I was right. I have changed in what I can do — fractions, ratios, negative numbers, equations — but I have grown more in how I work: I check my own answers, I can explain my thinking to someone else, and I expect hard problems to take more than one try.

practice.commonMistake: Treating your math story as finished — writing the same answers you wrote in Lesson 1-1 instead of looking for what actually changed. The story grows and evolves; a retrospective that copies September has missed the point.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Which statement best captures this lesson's end-of-year summary of 'Math is Mine'?
choices: We are all doers of math in daily life, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Math belongs only to the students who mastered every unit this year
A math story is written once in September and never changes
Math stops mattering once the school year ends
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes both claims: everyone is a doer of math in daily life, and our stories keep growing and evolving as we advance.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has two parts: doers of math, and stories that keep growing.
Which option keeps both?

questions.stem: A bead pattern goes A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. What is the pattern unit?
choices: A, B, C
A
A, B, C, A, B, C
A, A, B, B, C, C
questions.explanation: The pattern unit is the shortest chunk that repeats — here, A, B, C.
questions.stemEs: Un patrón de cuentas va A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. ¿Cuál es la unidad del patrón?
choicesEs: A, B, C, A, B, C
A, A, B, B, C, C
questions.explanationEs: La unidad del patrón es el trozo más corto que se repite — aquí, A, B, C.

questions.stem: A bead pattern repeats the unit A, B, C. What is the 10th bead?
choices: A
B
C
There is no 10th bead
questions.explanation: Three beads repeat, and 10 = 3 × 3 + 1. After 9 beads the unit restarts, so the 10th is A.
questions.stemEs: Un patrón de cuentas repite la unidad A, B, C. ¿Cuál es la 10.ª cuenta?
questions.explanationEs: Se repiten tres cuentas, y 10 = 3 × 3 + 1. Después de 9 cuentas la unidad vuelve a empezar, así que la 10.ª es A.

questions.stem: What makes a repeating design predictable?
choices: A pattern unit that repeats in the same order
Using many different colors
Making every piece a different size
Leaving gaps between the pieces
questions.explanation: Once you know the pattern unit and its order, you can predict any position in the design.
questions.stemEs: ¿Qué hace predecible un diseño que se repite?
choicesEs: Una unidad de patrón que se repite en el mismo orden
Hacer cada pieza de un tamaño distinto
questions.explanationEs: Una vez que conoces la unidad del patrón y su orden, puedes predecir cualquier posición del diseño.

questions.stem: A tile border repeats a 4-tile unit 6 times. How many tiles are in the border?
questions.explanation: The 4 tiles repeat 6 times, so multiply: 4 × 6 = 24. Adding gives 10.
questions.stemEs: Un borde de mosaicos repite una unidad de 4 mosaicos 6 veces. ¿Cuántos mosaicos hay en el borde?
questions.explanationEs: Los 4 mosaicos se repiten 6 veces, así que multiplica: 4 × 6 = 24. Sumar da 10.

parallelPractice.stem: Find 5% of 80 using a model or equation.
hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
Start like this: Write 5% as a decimal: 0.05.
parallelPractice.explanation: Write 5% as a decimal: 0.05. Find the percent amount: 80 × 0.05 = 4.
parallelPractice.stemEs: Encuentra el 5% de 80 usando un modelo o una ecuación.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta. ¿Qué te pide encontrar exactamente?
Usa el modelo visual y completa un paso a la vez.
Empieza así: Escribe 5% como decimal: 0.05.
parallelPractice.explanationEs: Escribe 5% como decimal: 0.05. Encuentra la cantidad del porcentaje: 80 × 0.05 = 4.
